notable.name: Spanish
notable.note: large speaker population; bilingual English/Spanish signage common in border states (Southwest) and Florida

terrainDescription.zh: 國土極為遼闊，涵蓋沙漠（西南部）、高山（洛磯山脈、阿帕拉契山脈）、大平原農業帶（中西部）、溫帶森林（東部）與都市化沿海地帶；此處僅列全國通用特徵，各州地理與氣候差異極大，區域細節待日後擴充。
terrainDescription.en: Vast and geographically extreme — desert in the Southwest, mountains (Rockies, Appalachians), agricultural plains across the Midwest, temperate forest in the East, and dense urban coastlines. This covers only nationwide common features; regional/state-level variation is substantial and left for future expansion.

plate.color: design and background color are set independently by each of the 50 states (+ DC) — no single national look; black or dark text is typical but varies; this is a nationwide summary only, state-level plate design is out of scope here
plate.shape: rectangular, ~305×152mm; most states require rear plate only, roughly 31 states also require a front plate — varies by state, not verified to state level in this pass

roadInfra.bollardStyle: No single national bollard style — thin white or orange flexible delineator posts are common on highway shoulders, but design varies by state DOT; nationwide summary only, not verified state-by-state

utilityPole.transformerMount: Wooden poles with a horizontal crossarm carrying pin-type insulators are the dominant style nationwide; grey cylindrical pole-mounted single-phase transformers ("cans") partway up the pole are a very common, recognizable feature; regional variation (steel/concrete poles in some areas, undergrounded lines in dense cities) exists but isn't detailed here

historicalContext.zh: 英語因英國殖民歷史成為事實上的通用語言，聯邦層級並無法定官方語言；西班牙語人口持續增長，尤其在西南與南部各州，部分地區可見英西雙語路牌。
historicalContext.en: English became the de facto lingua franca through British colonial history; there is no federally codified official language. The Spanish-speaking population continues to grow, especially in the Southwest and South, producing bilingual English/Spanish signage in some areas.
